Summary description of the proposed organizational change The proposed change is to transfer the Department of Landscape Architecture from the College of Arts and Sciences to the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
The transfer will result in the relocation of a design program that offers an accredited BLA and educates students about profession of landscape architecture and focuses many of its project assignments on addressing issues of community and urban design, sustainable design and coastal resilience, and ecological and environmental design and planning.
At any given moment, the average number of students in the department averages between 55 and 70.
It should be noted that our sophomore class is typically filled and capped at 20.
Our average graduating class of is 16.6 over 10 years.
LAR will also bring to the college an existing Graduate Certificate in Community Planning, minors in both CPL and LAR and the desire to create a new master's program.

This relocation will strengthen the college by adding a design unit with visualization capabilities and a track record for collaborative problem-solving and award-winning service-learning studio project.
The move will enhance LAR'S positioning for research, and it will make it easier to collaborate with the 2

existing college's disciplines, many of which are addressing the same issues. In addition, faculty in LAR and CELS are already involved in interdisciplinary exchanges through team teaching, studio classes and invited lectures and critiques. Background: Collaborative Discipline - Landscape architecture is a collaborative discipline that interacts with diverse fields and disciplines, such as art and architecture, planning and engineering, and the natural and social sciences.
It is profession whose practitioners and students work to solve problems that affect our communities and neighborhoods, natural and built environments and coastal cities and towns.
Its students learn to use planning and design, art and technology, and construction and visualization while working with professionals and stakeholders with a range of skills.
Their work requires that they develop skills in design, CAD, GIS, modeling.
Photoshop and other visualization technologies for developing and illustrating plans and proposals for neighborhoods, parks and streets and coastal communities.
The students also learn to work in teams, with different disciplines and with stakeholders on challenging projects around the state.

INTER INSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: The organizational change should be consistent with all policies of the Council on Postsecondary Education pertaining to the coordination and collaboration between public institutions of higher education. 1.
The Bachelor of Landscape Architecture program is the only degree of its kind offered at any public institution within the State.
There are four accredited BLA institution), University of Massachusetts, University of Connecticut and University of Rhode Island.

Because of their distant locations from each other, there is little interaction that occurs between these schools.
Proposed changes will have no significance to the structure of the institution, nor do they change the opportunity for students from Rhode Island to receive an accredited degree, which is one requirement for becoming licensed in the state as a landscape architect.
Statistically, there are 97 accredited landscape architecture programs in the US and 27 institutions have a single degree of BLA or BSLA. 2.
There are no cooperative arrangements with other institutions to provide landscape architecture classes or faculty to other institutions.
The Department of Landscape Architecture BLA degree is associated with the New England Regional Student Program offering tuition incentives to students from Maine, Vermont and New Hampshire.
This status will not change. 3.
There are no external affiliations associated with the Department of Landscape Architecture.

PROGRAM INFORMATION 1.

Presently, the School of Professional and Continuing Studies offers four tracks within the Bachelors of Interdisciplinary Studies (BIs) program: Applied Communication, Business Institutions, Health Services Administration, and Human Studies.

Due to a trifecta of reasons including (a) accreditation issues, (b) courses no longer in existence, and (C) courses no Ionger available at the Feinstein Providence Campus, we propose to integrate the four tracks into a single General Studies program. (Ultimately, if approved, this would enable students at URI to pursue and earn two Bachelors of Interdisciplinary Studies degrees: Learner Designed (Three Minor Major) as well as this re-formulated General Studies degree.
The proposed General Studies program is specifically designed for and tailored to meet the needs of students who transfer or re-admit to the University with a substantial number of credits (i.e., 60 or more credits).
Currently, no program provides these students with an efficient path to graduation.
Our goal with the General Studies program is to maximize their credits and integrate their learning from previously-taken courses.
These students are opting for competitive institutions due to the length of time it would take them to graduate and the ultimate cost of their educational pursuits.
Currently, if they were to attend URl, they would need to study within a traditional program and earn those major-specific credits.

Many of their previously-earned credits would not be viable ultimately resulting in a lengthy duration, higher educational costs, and earned credits being perceived as "worthless".
We believe this program change to establish a BIS General Studies would be remarkably beneficial to students who are pursuing other institutions with similar programs.
The General Studies program supports students who: Enter URI with substantial (e.g., 60+), yet scattered credits.
These students would be able to fulfill degree requirements in two or three semesters, as compared to four or more semesters in other programs. 02-25-2021 akt

Are seeking a broad, yet individualized, interdisciplinary degree.
The General Studies program is structured to support students who have limited interest in currently available majors and want to craft a learning experience that resonates with their professional pursuits.
Have a primary focus on earning a degree quickly, regardless of major designation.
Many students who will pursue this degree are seeking a highly flexible program that accepts a high number of credits.
This degree option will meet the demands of students focused on speedy degree completion, evening course options, and the viability of scattered credits Want to complete their degree solely on the Feinstein Providence campus.
As adult-learners, they want to study with other adult-learners in face-to-face classrooms.
More so, This degree can be earned, in full, by taking courses at the Feinstein Providence Campus where we guarantee night-time and weekend courses which align with their work, family, and community obligations.
We believe this General Studies program would be remarkably beneficial to the University of Rhode Island and the College of Education and Professional Studies.

For example: · We would attract and serve a specific student population who are otherwise enrolling With this additional student population, we could boost enrollments in courses our other School of Professional Studies s majors (e.g, Nonprofit Administration, Professional Leadership Studies) as well as courses offered at the Feinstein Providence Campus by other Colleges, Schools, and Departments.
This major can operate without any additional costs.
Students would be able to fulfill their major and general education requirements by taking courses currently offered.
No new courses will need to be developed and Kingston-based programs would not be obligated to reserve spaces for Interdisciplinary Studies students.

We would be able to maintain the flexibility of the former four Bl S tracks for our adult- learner student population, while ensuring that all classes offered at the Feinstein Providence Campus fulfill requirements towards graduation. (*Please note, all currently enrolled students in the four BIS tracks would be taught out to earn those degrees.) Election of Officers. 5.1 In February of each academic year, the Senate shall elect for the following academic year a Vice President/President-elect who shall serve one year as Vice President/President-elect and a second, consecutive year as President.
Senators who are elected to serve this two-year leadership position, as described, shall remain full members of the Faculty Senate as representatives of their colleges for the duration of their service even if the two-year position exceeds the three-year term limit as a Senator (Appendix C, section 2.1).
The outgoing President whose term has expired shall continue as an ex officio member of the Executive Committee for a period of one year after expiration of the term as President, and shall be considered ex officio member of the Faculty Senate during the same year.
At its the organizational meeting in May of the newly constituted Senate, the Senate shall elect at least one senator for a one-year term on the Executive Committee.
In order to ensure continuity, the remaining three members of the Executive Committee shall be elected to serve for two years.

To stagger their terms, two of the 2-year term members shall be elected on even numbered years and the other 2-year term member on odd numbered years. #04-05-25, #10-11-29, #14-15-25, #20-21-5 6.1 Appointing Committee Members and Committee Chairs.
The Executive Committee, with the consent of the Senate, shall appoint for three-year terms faculty members and for two-year terms chairpersons of standing committees and subcommittees to replace those faculty members and chairpersons whose terms are about to expire.
These appointments shall be on a staggered basis so that one-third of the members of each committee are replaced each year and so that the chairpersons of half the committees are replaced each year.
Besides students (see By-laws 4.13), only elected Faculty Senate members shall be eligible to serve on standing Faculty Senate committees.
At Within two weeks of adjournment of the newly elected senators shall submit to the Senate President lists of at least three standing committees and/or subcommittees on which they are willing to serve.
These committees and/or subcommittees may be listed in an order of priority.
A newly elected senator who will have to miss the organizational meeting shall send May organizational Faculty Senate meeting of the newly constituted Senate, all

the list to the Faculty Senate office prior to the organizational meeting, or as soon as possible thereafter.
The Executive Committee shall use these lists to nominate, during the summer, for Faculty Senate approval (see below), new committee and subcommittee members for three-year terms to replace those committee members whose terms are about to expire.
When the term of a committee or subcommittee chair is about to expire, a new chair shall also be nominated for a two-year term (see By-laws 4.13).
Ideally, chairs shall be chosen from those committee and/or subcommittee members whose remaining Senate terms are two years; committee chairs may, however, also be chosen from newly elected senators.
While efforts will be made to nominate senators for a committee and/or subcommittee included in the list a senator submitted, there is no guarantee that this will be possible.
If the only committee slots available for a senator differ from the committees contained in the list the senator has submitted, the Faculty Senate Coordinator shall contact the senator to determine whether he or she is willing to serve on a committee on which a slot is not yet filled.

When the list of new members and new committee chairs is presented, at the first Fall Semester Senate meeting, to the Senate for approval, the Senate's action shall be limited to consenting to the nominees for each committee or to referring the matter back to the Executive Committee.
Unless stated otherwise in the description of an individual committee, committee chairs shall be entitled to have their normal duties reduced by one-third, normal duties being specified in Article IV, paragraph 2, of the Constitution of the Faculty Senate, and entitlement shall follow automatically upon appointment.

In accordance with Article VII, 1 and 2 of the Constitution, the amendment was subject to ratification "by an affirmative vote of two-thirds of the General Faculty, excluding abstentions." The referendum of the General Faculty was conducted from April 26, 2021 until May 3, 2021 via electronic ballots. The results of the referendum are: Affirmative votes 310 Negative votes 48 Abstentions 3 Total votes 361 Total votes, excluding abstentions 358 Excluding abstentions, of the votes cast, 87% were affirmative: the amendment has been ratified. The Faculty Senate will now forward this Bill to President Dooley for his approval. Once it is approved, the modified Faculty Senate membership and apportionment system will take effect for the Spring 2022 apportionment calculations and college elections.

GRADUATE CURRICULAR REPORT #2020-2021-4 GRADUATE COUNCIL FEBRUARY 8, 2021 FACULTY SENATE FEBRUARY 18, 2021 SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate The Graduate Council approved the proposal to create an accelerated Online Master of Public Administration (MPA) and forwards it to the Faculty Senate with a recommendation for approval. One of the structural revisions and innovations of the online MPA program is the creation of three certificate programs that offer students with both core training in public administration and policy but also specializations mirroring the Public Management and Policy Analysis concentrations in the current program. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) Since its founding in the 1970’s, the mission of the Master of Public Administration (MPA) program at the University of Rhode Island is to instill public values, knowledge, and expertise to

2 prepare our graduates to solve problems related to governance, nonprofit management, and policy with integrity, professionalism, and excellence to improve our communities and society.
To train our students to meet the challenges of the 21st Century, the MPA program is embarking on a series of program revisions and a transition to a fully online program to meet the current and anticipated future needs from employers and various stakeholders across Rhode Island, the region, and nationally.
Although the MPA program will transition to a fully online, accelerated (7-week) format and replace its current blended, 14-week modality, the MPA program will retain many of its successful core features, including the requirement that MPA graduates earn 36 credits.
The accelerated online MPA program also incorporates new curricular innovations that will expand student recruitment and student flexibility.
Additionally, the programmatic and curricular revisions outlined in this proposal are critical for the program to become accredited by the Network of Schools of Public Policy, Affairs, and Administration (NASPAA) – a long-standing goal of the program – in the coming years.

One of the structural revisions and innovations of the online MPA program is the creation of three certificate programs that offer students with both core training in public administration and policy but also specializations mirroring the Public Management and Policy Analysis concentrations in the current program.
The three 12-credit graduate certificates in the online MPA program are: the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy, Public Management, and Policy Analysis.
Students in the online MPA program will need to complete the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy graduate certificate, at least one of the other two MPA graduate certificates, earn at least 36 credits, and complete the capstone course to complete their MPA degree.
The core certificate that forms the basis for the MPA online program is the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy.

Students completing this certificate program will have an opportunity to learn about the historical and theoretical foundations of public administration and policy (PSC 501), ethical decision-making strategies (PSC 504), diversity and inclusion in the public sector (PSC 502), and an elective course focused on developing core skills or experience for a career in government, non-profits, or policy.
All students who want to earn their MPA degree will be required to complete this graduate certificate.
In addition to the certificate in Public Administration and Policy, students choosing to graduate with an MPA degree can choose to complete either one or two additional MPA-offered certificates that form the basis of an added credential or specialization that will make graduates competitive in the job market.
The first is a certificate in Public Management.
The coursework required for this certificate will help students become competitive applicants for positions requiring financial and budgetary expertise (PSC 506 & PSC 507), leadership skills, knowledge of administrative law and procedure (PSC 573), and the management of agency personnel (PSC 503).

Currently, there is an acute need in many cities and towns for Finance Director positions, which can be a town or city’s highest paid municipal position.
Additionally, these are skills increasingly

3 sought by nonprofit organizations. By creating a certificate program, we hope to fulfill this workforce need in the state of Rhode Island and beyond by offering incumbent employees and new students the opportunity to develop a competency in Public Management. Our aim is to have incumbent workers trained so that they will have opportunities for advancement, and their advancement will, in turn, create entry-level opportunities for others pursuing a certificate in Public Management or our students completing the MPA program. The second of these optional certificates is the Policy Analysis certificate. The coursework required for this certificate will help students develop research and analytical capabilities (PSC 583 & PSC 510), evaluate public programs (PSC 505), and navigate the public policy process (PSC 524 & PSC 510). These skills will allow them to become effective at shaping public policy either within public agencies or as part of a broader policymaking process. Students pursuing this certificate will develop skills that will allow them to be policy advocates, policy researchers, and/or communication specialists. The underlying philosophy of the URI MPA online program is that its modular design will guide students along pathways that will allow them to align their graduate study with their career ambitions. MPA graduates will have earned no less than 36 credits while completing the program. All students completing the full 36-credit program will: • Complete the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy (12 credits);

4 • Complete either the Policy Analysis certificate (12 credits) and/or the Public Management certificate (12 credits); • Complete the remaining 12 elective credits if only one certificate program is chosen between the Policy Analysis certificate or the Public Management certificate. Graduates may choose to pursued a stackable certificate in another program to add alongside the two MPA certificates. Upon approval of the online MPA program, the Department of Political Science will develop an Advanced Bachelors-to-Master (ABM) program for undergraduates seeking to enter the MPA program by completing twelve credits during their senior year. These courses would not be offered by URI Online but are instead delivered through our traditional 14-week program. These courses will include: • PSC 402-Environmental Politics and Policy (4 credits), • PSC 405-Politics of Health and Aging (4 credits), • PSC 590-Internship in Public Administration (4 credits), • 4 credit policy or public-management related courses. Another potential entry into the MPA online program will occur at the certificate level where students may decide to enroll in the MPA program during or following the completion of one of the certificate programs. State the program objectives.
The mission of the URI MPA Online program is to instill public service values, knowledge, and expertise to prepare graduates to solve problems with integrity, professionalism, and excellence to improve our communities and society.
Goal 1: to lead and manage in governance. 1.1 Describe and analyze the theoretical, legal, and conceptual foundations of the fields of public administration and public policy. 1.2 Gather information and analyze the internal and external environments surrounding public and nonprofit agencies to develop leadership or policy strategies.
Goal 2: to participate in and contribute to the policy process. 2.1 Identify, diagnose, and convey to policymakers real policy or management-related problems and solutions that affect the policy process, public management, or public policy outcomes.

Goal 3: to analyze, synthesize, think critically, solve problems and make decisions. 3.1 Apply appropriately tailored analytical skills to interpret and solve real policy or management- related problems.
Goal 4: to articulate and apply a public service perspective. 4.1 Inform and advise policymakers about policy or management-related problems in ways that advance the public interest, respect the rule of law, promote democratic participation, and treat people fairly. 4.2 Demonstrate personal integrity and inspire public confidence and trust in public service by developing, individually and in teams, work products that adhere to the highest standards of professional conduct.

6 Goal 5: to communicate and interact productively with a diverse and changing workforce and citizenry. 5.1 Effectively communicate with multiple audiences in policy or public management related settings. 5.2 Collaborate with a diverse collection of stakeholders to solve public policy and public management-related problems.

What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
The design of the MPA online program is not only aligned with NASPAA accreditation guidelines but also meets the growing workplace needs in Rhode Island, the region, and nationally.
To gauge the current and future hiring needs of employers in the public and nonprofit sectors, the MPA director, Dr.
Aaron Ley, conducted a series of meetings with key government and nonprofit stakeholders throughout the state over the last two years.
The meetings included the Rhode Island League of Cities and Towns, the Rhode Island City and Town Managers Association, and various other state agencies like the Rhode Island Secretary of State’s office, among others.

These meetings revealed the growing need of individuals with management and finance backgrounds because employees currently holding these positions are beginning to reach the age of retirement.
These discussions were confirmed through the Director’s own anecdotal experience in Bristol where the town’s finance director chose to take a position closer to home.
During that hiring process for the replacement, the town observed that very few people in its applicant pool were qualified to fill this position.
Nationally, municipal Finance Director positions are among some of the highest paid municipal employees.
In order to address this workforce need, and as part of our migration of the MPA program to an online format, we are proposing the development of a stackable Public Management Certificate that will allow our students to enter our program in order to develop skills relating to public budgeting and finance.

This will allow incumbent workers and entry-level workers to quickly earn a competency in public management by completing a suite of four courses to fulfill this certificate, while also giving them the option of remaining in the program to complete the MPA Online program by completing the other 24 credits.
We hope that the training of incumbent workers will create opportunities for their advancement, which will create entry-level opportunities for others pursuing a certificate in Public Management or our students completing the MPA program.
This stackable certificate can be used by MPA students desiring a special competency in the area of public management, or for students in other graduate programs wanting to use their remaining electives to gain public management skills.

7 These information gathering meetings on public and nonprofit sector workforce development needs also revealed a need for the upskilling of incumbent workers and the training of more entry-level employees with analytical skills relating to public policy.
One case in point was a conversation with Rob Rock, the Director of Elections at the Rhode Island Secretary of State’s (SOS) office, and an alum of the URI MPA program.
Mr.
Rock stated that the high priority legislation that is being pursued by the SOS office requires a lot of research and analysis of data.
His observations were confirmed during conversations with Rhode Island Secretary of State Nellie Gorbea.
To fulfill this workforce need, we are proposing the creation of a stackable Policy Analysis certificate, which can be pursued by MPA students in conjunction with the Public Management certificate or by students in other programs who are wanting to use their electives to pursue a credential that bolsters the student’s policy analytical skills. b.
Provide information on jobs available as a result of successfully completing the certificate or degree: job titles, job outlook/growth, and salaries.

Students completing an MPA degree with the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy, along with a certificate in Policy Analysis and/or Public Management will be competitive applicants for positions requiring financial and budgetary expertise, leadership skills, knowledge of administrative law and procedure, the management of agency personnel, policy and grant writing, and analytical skills.
Currently, while there are no data regarding salaries for employees earning certificates, there is extensive survey research that exists on salaries of alumni holding an MPA/MPP degree.
According to a 2018 survey administered by the Network of Schools of Public Policy, Affairs, and Administration (NASPAA), over half of all graduates surveyed with an MPA made over $65,000 after three years of having earned the degree (https://www.naspaa.org/data-center/alumni-survey).
Of those receiving an MPP/MPA degree, 48% were employed in government careers, 22% in nonprofit careers, and 18% were employed in the private sector.

Four percent of respondents completing the 2018 survey were unemployed, while 8% of respondents chose “other.” An ideal federal placement for a student with an MPA and a certificate in Public Management, Policy Analysis, or the Graduate Certificate in Public Administration and Policy would be as a “Contract Specialist” at the Department of Navy’s Naval Undersea Warfare Center.
The salary for such a position is $64,873 to $111,062 per year.
The basic requirements for contracting positions include a Bachelor’s Degree and 24 semester hours of finance, legal, and management-related training.
